🚀 We're Hiring: SAP SRM Functional Consultant (FTE) 🚀
LTM is looking for an experienced SAP SRM Functional Consultant to join our team on-site in Delhi! If you have deep expertise in SAP SRM procurement processes along with exposure to modern SAP AI tools, we want to hear from you.

📌 Role Details:
Job Code: TRX-26167
Company: LTM
Experience: 7+ Years
Location: Delhi (Client Location)
Work Mode: Work From Office – 5 Days a Week (No WFH)
Employment Type: Full-Time (FTE)
Compensation: ₹18 LPA

💼 What We’re Looking For (Mandatory):
7+ years of SAP SRM functional consulting experience with at least 2 end-to-end implementations.
Strong command over SAP SRM procurement: SUS, Shopping Cart/PO processing, Strategic Sourcing, Contract Management, Supplier Evaluation, and Service Procurement.
Solid understanding of SAP ECC MM integration and Classic, Extended Classic, Standalone, & Service Procurement scenarios.
Hands-on experience with ALE/IDoc, workflow configuration, BRF, Web Dynpro, and portal-based procurement.
Proven track record in production support, enhancements, UAT, deployment, and stakeholder management.
Mandatory exposure to: AI/GenAI, ML Algorithms, Prompt Engineering, SAP Business AI for eProcurement, SAP IP-Tools, SAP Joule for Consultants (J4C), and SAP Signavio – Functional.

🎯 Key Responsibilities:
Analyze business requirements and design/configure end-to-end SAP SRM solutions (org structures, business partners, product categories, workflows).
Manage SAP SRM & SAP ECC MM integration and support sourcing, RFQs, bids, contracts, confirmations, and invoices.
Partner with technical teams on enhancements, interfaces, reports, forms, and workflows.
Handle production support within SLA timelines, lead UAT, user training, and functional documentation.

✨ Good to Have:
SAP SRM Certification & SAP Ariba integration experience.
Exposure to S/4HANA procurement, SAP Fiori, and SAP MDG.
Domain background in Manufacturing, Retail, FMCG, or Chemicals, plus procurement compliance/audit knowledge.

📩 How to Apply: Interested candidates can send their updated CV to virajnarkar07@gmail.com.Please ensure you mention "TRX-26167 – SAP SRM Functional Consultant" in the email subject line.

WE ARE HIRING – Sales Executive / Business Development Executive​

Join SenseTime Middle East Technology Limited and be part of the future of AI-powered innovation!​

📍 Location: Abu Dhabi, UAE
🏢 Department: Sales / Business Development
🌍 Market Coverage: UAE & Middle East
🗣️ Language: Arabic & English (Mandatory)​

We are looking for an energetic, ambitious, proactive, and results-driven sales professional to promote our AI products, innovative technology solutions, digital ticketing systems, and smart guest experience solutions across the UAE and wider Middle East.​

We are particularly interested in candidates with sales or business development experience within the ticketing, entertainment, theme park, leisure attractions, and hospitality industries.​

Key Responsibilities:​

• Identify, develop, and pursue new business opportunities.
• Promote AI-powered solutions, digital ticketing platforms, smart visitor management, and guest experience technologies.
• Build strong relationships with theme park operators, entertainment companies, government entities, and key decision-makers.
• Conduct client meetings, product presentations, and demonstrations.
• Manage lead generation, prospecting, sales pipelines, and customer follow-ups.
• Prepare commercial proposals, negotiate contracts, and close business opportunities.
• Achieve sales targets, revenue objectives, and business development KPIs.
• Represent the company at industry events, exhibitions, and networking activities.​

Requirements:​

• Bachelor's degree in Business Administration, Sales, Marketing, or a related field.
• Fluency in Arabic and English is mandatory.
• Previous experience in sales, business development, or account management.
• Experience in ticketing, entertainment, theme parks, leisure attractions, or hospitality is highly preferred.
• Experience selling AI, IT, software, ticketing platforms, access control systems, or digital technology solutions is an advantage.
• Strong industry connections across the UAE and Middle East are highly desirable.
• Excellent communication, presentation, and negotiation skills.
• Strong hunter mentality with a passion for generating new business.
• Proactive, commercially driven, resilient, and target-oriented.
• UAE driving license and willingness to travel are preferred.​

If you are passionate about technology, innovation, sales, and transforming the entertainment and attractions industry, we would love to hear from you!​

A great new paper from MIT and Microsoft
Shows GitHub Copilot cut junior software engineer hiring by about 40%
Generally the paper finds GitHub Copilot cuts hiring of junior coders at large firms, while worker exits and senior hiring stay flat.
Firms that adopt AI early already hire and grow differently, so simple comparisons can't show what AI coding tools do to jobs. Earlier studies on this question reached conflicting answers.
They tracked 5,414 multinational firms, covering 38% of US programmers, whose GitHub contract reviews were set before Copilot launched. Firms reviewed earlier adopted Copilot sooner, which created a natural experiment.
After 1 year, quarterly technical hiring fell 29% at firms pushed to adopt by their review date, with no rise in exits. Their junior software engineer hiring fell about 40%, while experienced engineer hiring held steady.
Before Copilot, 72% of junior tech hires went into coding-heavy roles. After adoption it was 52%, so entry-level hiring ends up split about evenly between coding-heavy and less coding-heavy roles.

Want a fully remote job in 2026? Stop applying like everyone else. Start proving you can do the job.
Thousands of professionals are searching for remote opportunities.
They are updating their CVs.
Applying to job boards.
Sending applications to companies hiring remotely.
But here's what most candidates are missing:
Companies don't just hire people who want to work remotely. They hire people they trust to deliver results without being micromanaged.
So, instead of sending another CV, use AI to build proof of your abilities.
Here's a 5-step strategy to stand out:
1. Find companies that are actually hiring remotely.
Start with the careers pages of companies such as:
↳ Zapier
↳ Automattic
↳ GitLab
↳ HubSpot
But don't stop at the job title.
Check:
Eligible countries and locations
Required working hours and time zones
Skills and experience required
Employment type and contract conditions
Remember: Fully remote doesn't necessarily mean work from anywhere.
2. Create your own remote work simulation.
This is where AI becomes your advantage.
Copy the job description into ChatGPT and use this prompt:
"Create a realistic one-day work assignment for this role. Include the task, expected deliverables, deadline, required tools, and measurable success criteria."
For example:
↳ Zapier: Build an automated workflow.
↳ Automattic: Create a customer support knowledge base.
↳ GitLab: Improve technical documentation.
↳ HubSpot: Build a sample email marketing campaign.
Complete the assignment yourself, using AI as your assistant.
Don't just generate an answer. Demonstrate your actual skills.
3. Show recruiters how you think.
A finished project is valuable.
But showing your thought process makes it even more powerful.
Record a 3-minute Loom video explaining:
↳ What problem you were solving.
↳ How you approached the task.
↳ Which tools you used and why.
↳ What challenges you faced.
↳ What results you achieved.
Use Loom AI to generate a written summary of your walkthrough.
4. Use AI to evaluate your work.
Upload your completed project and summary to Claude.
Ask it to evaluate your work based on:
Technical accuracy
Communication skills
Problem-solving ability
Attention to detail
Independent decision-making
Then ask:
"What would make this submission stand out to a hiring manager recruiting for a fully remote position?"
Improve your weak points before submitting.
5. Build a proof-based application package.
Instead of sending only a traditional CV, include:
↳ Your tailored CV
↳ A self-created sample project
↳ A 3-minute video walkthrough
↳ A concise written project summary
Now your application does something different.
It doesn't just tell recruiters what you can do.
It gives them evidence.
Here's the bigger lesson:
In a competitive remote job market, your ability to demonstrate your skills can become your biggest advantage.
AI isn't just helping you write better applications.
It's helping you build a portfolio, simulate real work, identify weaknesses, and communicate your value.
Stop saying you're ready for remote work. Start showing why you're the right person to hire.

10 Compliance Gaps Where the AI Industry Is Failing in India

1. Personal data used for training (DPDP Act 2023)
- No policies in corporate which prevents employee for reasonable use of personal information 

- Scraped or customer data goes into models with no notice or consent. Neither lawful basis recorded, no retention or deletion rule.
   

2. Copyright in training data (Copyright Act 1957)
   - Books, news, images, and code are used without licences
   - India has no clear text-and-data-mining exception, so the exposure is real
   

3. Deepfakes and synthetic content (IT Act and Intermediary Rules)
   - No labelling of AI-generated content
   - Slow takedown of impersonation and non-consensual content
   - MeitY has issued advisories on this, and labelling rules have been proposed. 

4. Personality and publicity rights
   - Voices, faces, and likenesses are cloned without permission
   - Delhi and Bombay High Courts have granted injunctions to public figures against AI misuse

5. Vendor and client contracts

Corporates are signing contract with:
   - Unlimited liability for model errors
   - No clarity on who owns outputs, fine-tuned models, and customer data
   - No disclaimer on accuracy or on the use of third-party models

6. Open-source and model licence breaches
   - Llama, Mistral, and similar licences carry usage restrictions
   - Founders ship commercial products without reading the terms
   - Licence attribution and field-of-use limits are ignored

7. Cybersecurity and CERT-In duties
   - No 6-hour incident reporting process
   - Prompt injection, data leakage, and model theft are not covered by the security policy
   - Logs are not kept for 180 days as the directions require

8. Employment and IP ownership
   - Engineers' code and datasets are not assigned to the company
   - Contractors and annotators work without IP clauses or NDAs
   - Employees paste confidential data into public AI tools

9. Sector rules ignored
   - Finance: RBI model-risk and fair-lending expectations for AI-driven credit
   - Health: AI in diagnosis can attract medical device rules and patient-data duties
   - Hiring and edtech: bias, children's data, and consent gaps

10. Governance and transparency
    - No AI policy, no model inventory, no human-review step for high-risk decisions
    - No bias testing or documentation

Many recent college graduates aren't using their degrees

“Right now, there’s lots of uncertainty and that’s freezing the labor market,” said Jeff Strohl, research professor and senior adviser of the Georgetown University Center on Education and the Workforce. “And recent college grads pay the price.”
The Post talked to a dozen recent college graduates in their 20s and 30s who are underemployed or unemployed. Most said this isn’t the job market they expected after doing what they had long been told was the best path to a career: going to college, completing internships and earning degrees. Plus, AI has fundamentally changed the way job applications work, leaving them caught in an automation vortex.
Underemployed college graduates also say that any job is better than no job. But working a low-paid administrative, retail or infrequent gig job isn’t exactly what they had in mind.
“It’s clearly just a really bad market on top of a really antiquated way we look at jobs versus how jobs are acquired,” said Ethan Maas, a 23-year-old who graduated last December with a bachelor’s in computer engineering from Virginia Tech. He’s now working contract IT jobs that usually last for a couple days at a time.
While it’s not unusual for new grads to take awhile to find their first job or start in low-paying roles on their way to a career, recent college graduates are dealing with disruptions past generations didn’t face, economists and labor market experts say.
Strohl calls it a “perfect storm.” The pandemic has had a cumulative effect, disrupting some internship opportunities and making it harder for graduates from the last few years to find jobs, meaning the number of entry-level workers looking for jobs has piled up.
“The effects of the pandemic itself (on recent graduate hiring) are probably long gone, but it caused a ripple in the entry labor market,” Strohl said. “It slowed things down, it made a bit of a backup in the drain.”
The second Trump term brought new tariffs, making companies more cautious to hire. It also brought DOGE, the federal government cost-cutting initiative that led to hundreds of thousands of workers losing or leaving their jobs and billions of dollars of cuts to research grants, resulting in fewer job opportunities.
Recent college graduate Destiny Hurtado, 22, is working part-time and said she’s been passed over for candidates with more years of employment history, even when the job listing did not require prior experience.

Hurtado graduated from Lehman College in the Bronx in May with a degree in art focusing on design and a minor in marketing. She has been looking for jobs for about six hours each day, she said. For now, she’s designing fliers for the school of arts and humanities office at her alma mater, a part-time job she started while still studying.
She likes the work but needs something full-time to launch her career and move out of her grandparents’ house.
“The issue is that I need a stable job, I need more income,” she said.

If you're deliberately avoiding AI use in the workplace for fear of accelerating redundancy, you're probably making the situation worse for yourself.
 
Anthropic interviewed people at 58 companies about how they're adopting AI. Automation eliminated a role outright at two of them. At five, managers pushed out employees who refused to use AI. The bigger squeeze showed up in hiring, with two-thirds of the companies taking on fewer people.
 
For someone already in the job, holding out carries more risk than taking part as it hands the shape of the design to someone who might know how to automate your work but not how to amplify it. And with tools like Scribe's new Autocapture, your processes can get captured by the firm whether you help or not.
 
The people in the study who came out ahead automated their own work first. A contract administrator at a construction company automated their own data gathering and moved into rolling out AI across the firm. An engineer automated the alert tickets that filled his week, kept tuning the agent, and went on to build the Slack agent the company now runs on. A paralegal who had kept his AI method to himself shared it with the partners and took on responsibility for the firm's AI transition.
 
Every automated workflow needs someone who understands the work to build it and keep it running as things change. Firms are likely to hold on to such domain experts so you want to make sure that this person is you.

Your CFO is going to ask what AI actually saved marketing this year. Most teams will answer with one big number, and that's where they may lose the room.

The gap is real: 88% of organizations use AI in at least one function, but only 39% report any enterprise-level EBIT impact from it (McKinsey, State of AI). A better answer splits "AI savings" into three ledgers, each with its own proof:

1. Cash saved: invoices cancelled or reduced. It counts once the contract ends or renews lower, and finance signs it off.
2. Capacity freed: hours moved to work that actually shipped.
3. Unit cost: cost per asset, lead or campaign, measured over two full quarters.

It is a more honest story, and a more credible one. Klarna claimed about $10M a year in AI marketing savings in 2024, then by May 2025 its CEO said quality had suffered and it was hiring humans again.

Promise the ledgers and not the headline.

We have put the full CMO Mag playbook for the CFO conversation in the comments: stage gates, quality tripwires and how to present each ledger.

AI made building cheap. Now we're drowning in products and still pretty bad at knowing which ones actually work. That gap is the job. Understanding users is the moat.

Here are 3 things I recommend if you're a UXR in this era:

1. Study decisions, not just behaviour. Users are delegating more and more to AI. The real questions now are how people decide: what they hand over, what they keep, and why. Researchers who build interesting frameworks around that will be very valuable.

2. Use AI, but properly. AI-moderated tools are great for light-touch, low-cost questions to get you going. Nothing replaces face to face with the end user. Period. But you can run other things in parallel. Perspective Outset Listenlabs AI I have compared them all, reach out if you want to exchange notes.

3. Teach AI how you think. Pasting your Excel sheet link and asking Claude or Gemini to "create insights" is not it. It hasn't learnt enough from you. Show it how you synthesise, how you run thematic analysis, how you code, how you write. Start with a "write like me" skill: ask your favourite AI tool to analyse your channels and comms, build the skill, refine it, then use it for everything. "Sales are down. Cut everyone's pay by 20% next month."

Not without their agreement.

Salary is a term of the contract of service. One side cannot change it alone.

A pay cut imposed without the employee's agreement is a breach of his contract. A cut to his salary can be a breach that goes to the root of it.

That is the test for constructive dismissal. In Wong Chee Hong v Cathay Organisation (M) Sdn Bhd [1988] 1 MLJ 92, the Supreme Court adopted the contract test: where the employer commits a breach going to the root of the contract, the employee is entitled to treat himself as dismissed and leave.

He can then file a representation under section 20 of the Industrial Relations Act 1967 within 60 days. If the Industrial Court finds he was dismissed without just cause or excuse, it can order compensation and backwages.

Agreement has a floor too. Whatever is agreed, basic pay cannot go below the minimum wage of RM1,700 a month.

Asking employees to accept a pay cut is not a breach. Imposing one is.

What HR can do:

1. Explain the business position, and ask each employee to agree in writing to the amount and the period of the cut.
2. Look at other measures first, such as cutting overtime, freezing hiring or pausing discretionary benefits.
3. If an employee does not agree, take advice before you act. Do not cut his pay anyway.

A pay cut needs agreement. Imposed without it, it can become a constructive dismissal claim.

Lots of posts this week about #Claude being switched on inside Microsoft Copilot in #UK.
Some of it is spot on. Some of it isn't.
So here's a quick myth vs fact 👇

❌ Myth: Anthropic becomes a Microsoft sub-processor on 9 December.
✅ Fact: It already is. That happened back in January for most Microsoft customers. What changes on 9 December is the default for UK organisations that never made a choice.
❌ Myth: This is a big new Microsoft and Anthropic deal.
✅ Fact: It's an admin notice (MC1546435). Claude has been inside Copilot for a while. The UK was simply switched off by default until now.
❌ Myth: "Our data stays in the EU, so we're fine."
✅ Fact: EU customers are getting Claude processed inside the EU Data Boundary. UK customers aren't. Reports say UK processing happens in the US.
❌ Myth: You're forced to use it.
✅ Fact: Your admin can set it to no users, or only approved users, before or after the 9th.

Who in your business actually owns AI decisions?

Why internal structure is the foundation of business success.
Generating sales, hiring talented people and adopting new technologies are not enough. A business needs clearly defined departments, responsibilities, operational procedures and communication channels to function efficiently.
Without documented procedures, operational manuals and clearly assigned responsibilities, employees end up improvising, duplicating tasks and wasting valuable time.
A company should operate as an integrated system, not as an  independent one.
Especially in tourism, every department must understand the product being sold.
Supplier contracts, updated rates, confirmed services, availability and operational information must be properly documented and accessible.
How can a travel designer confidently sell a program if the product has not been fully developed, verified and structured?
Planning ahead, particularly for the following 12 months, is essential to commercial success.
Every department is part of the same engine
Sales, product development, contracting, reservations and operations are interconnected.
When one department lacks information or fails to respond, the entire process slows down.
Hiring an experienced professional does not mean that person can immediately perform at full capacity.
Expertise and know-how are valuable, but new employees also need structured training, documented procedures, system guidance, product knowledge and clearly defined responsibilities.
Without proper onboarding, valuable time is wasted searching for information and trying to understand processes that should already exist.
The professionalism, courtesy, responsiveness and quality of service offered to external clients must also exist internally.
Colleagues are internal customers. Cooperation, timely responses and effective communication are essential to operational excellence.
AI can improve individual tasks, automate processes and enhance productivity. However, it cannot compensate for missing procedures, undefined responsibilities or an unstructured product.
True digital transformation begins with understanding and improving how the organization operates.
The real foundation of growth
A company cannot remain indefinitely in an artisanal operating model based on improvisation and individual knowledge while expecting to compete and grow.
Sustainable development requires structure, planning, leadership, training, accountability and collaboration.

AI社員に「残業上限」。DeNAのAI社員は8日で52.6時間働いた / DeNA puts an overtime cap on its AI employees （English follows）

DeNAが11/20、「AI社員 by DeNA」を外部の企業向けに提供すると発表した模様です。

社内ではすでに30人のAI社員が、購買、情報システム、インフラ、IT品質管理、営業などの部門で働いているとのこと。会計システムの開発・保守チームのAI社員1人は、8営業日で52.6時間分、1日8時間勤務の約8割に相当する業務を担ったそうです。

面白いのは管理の言葉です。AIの稼働量（トークン使用量）を「勤務時間」、使いすぎを防ぐ上限を「残業の上限」として扱う、とあります。契約・発注の最終承認や採用の合否判定は人に残し、権限を超える作業は人に承認を求める設計とのこと。

個人的には、AIの費用は、トークンや従量課金という、経営や現場には見えにくい単位で語られてきたと思います。それを「勤務時間」と「残業」に置き換えると、AIの使いすぎを、人の働き方と同じ物差しで止められるようになりそうです。

ただ、上限を誰が決めるのか、上限に達したら止まるのか知らせるのかは、発表では公開されていません。人の残業は、上司が理由を見て認めるかどうかを判断します。AIの残業も、数字で止めるだけでなく、誰が「この仕事なら延長してよい」と判断するのかが、運用の肝になりそうですね。

あなたの現場では、AIの使いすぎに上限、ありますか？（ある／ない）

---

On Nov 20, DeNA announced that it will offer "AI Employee by DeNA" to other companies.

Inside DeNA, 30 AI employees already work in purchasing, IT, infrastructure, IT quality control and sales. One AI employee on the accounting system team did 52.6 hours of work in 8 business days. That is about 80% of an 8-hour workday.

The interesting part is the words. DeNA treats token usage as "working hours" and the usage limit as an "overtime cap." Final approval of contracts and orders, and hiring decisions, stay with people.

I think AI costs are usually explained in tokens and usage fees. Managers and teams cannot see them easily. If we call them working hours and overtime, we can manage AI with the same yardstick as people.

But the release does not say who sets the cap, or what happens when AI hits it. For people, a manager decides if overtime is OK. For AI, we will also need someone to decide when extra work is worth it.

Does your team have a cap on AI usage? Yes or no?
